About this simulation

This simulation shows a quantum-mechanical plane wave incident on a one-dimensional potential barrier (or step). You can watch the wave function ψ(x, t) evolve in time, and see the real part, imaginary part, and probability density |ψ|².

Adjust the barrier height U, half-width a, and particle energy E. The bottom panel plots the transmission probability T(E) versus energy; the current energy is marked on the curve. For a rectangular barrier centered on the origin, T = 1 at resonance energies above U.

Transmission (E < U, tunneling)

The formula below applies when particle energy is below the barrier height.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The beam and the barrier

Here’s our setup. A steady beam of electrons of energy E runs in from the left onto a rectangular barrier of height U and full width 2a. The upper panel shows you V(x) and E; the lower one draws Re(ψ), Im(ψ) and |ψ|² for the stationary wave. Right now E = 0.30 eV, U = 0.50 eV and a = 0.50 nm, so the beam sits below the barrier top.

2 · The classical beam

Let’s start simple and forget the wave for a moment. Imagine a classical beam aimed at the same barrier, with its energy raised steadily from well below U to well above it. What do you think the transmitted fraction does?

3 · A step instead of a barrier

Now back to the wave. Inside the barrier it decays, yet it still has some amplitude left at the far edge. So let’s swap the barrier for a step of the same height — same E, same U, but now there’s no far edge at all. What do you think the transmitted fraction will be?

4 · Raising the energy

Let’s go back to the rectangular barrier and sweep the beam energy upward, past U and beyond. Once you’re above the barrier top, what happens to the transmitted fraction?

5 · Where the peaks sit

One last experiment. With a = 0.50 nm, the first peak sits at E ≈ 0.88 eV. Now we’ll double the half-width to 1.00 nm and leave U unchanged. Where do you think the peaks will go?

The Physics

Quantum tunnelling · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A steady electron beam meets a barrier, and the sim draws the wave on both sides and reads off the transmitted fraction T and the reflected fraction R. The same mathematics governs the tunnel current of a scanning tunnelling microscope and alpha decay.

What you'll learn

  • How the wave behaves inside and beyond a barrier taller than the beam energy E.
  • How T depends on E, the height U and the width 2a.
  • How a single step differs from a barrier with two edges.
  • How T changes with E once E passes U.
The setup: a beam of energy E meets a barrier of height U and full width 2a.

What's on screen

  • Potential V(x) (red): 0 outside, U between x = −a and x = +a.
  • Beam energy E (dashed cyan), on the same axis.
  • Re ψ (blue): the real part of the wave, for x from −10 to 14 nm.
  • Im ψ (amber): the imaginary part of the wave.
  • |ψ|² (purple): probability density, relative to the incoming beam.
  • Transmission bar: T, R and T + R. The Guided Inquiry reveals it step by step.
  • T(E) spectrum and ANALYTICAL panels: T against E, and the formula in use.
See itRun the opening settings. Watch for: ripples in the purple curve left of the barrier, a much smaller wave to its right, and T = 3.86%.

03

The wave decays inside the barrier

Outside the barrier V = 0 and ψ is a travelling wave with wavenumber k. Inside, where U > E, the solutions are real exponentials with decay constant η:

The sim's units: m is the electron mass, k and η in nm⁻¹.

At the opening values k = 2.81 nm⁻¹, so the wavelength 2π/k is 2.24 nm, and η = 2.29 nm⁻¹. The amplitude inside falls by a factor e over 1/η = 0.44 nm.

A plane wave cannot be normalised, so the plot shows |ψ|² relative to the incoming beam, and T and R are ratios of probability current. The beam is a stationary state, so its time dependence is one phase factor:

The clock moves Re ψ and Im ψ. It cannot move |ψ|².
See itRun the opening settings and look at the three curves. Watch for: the blue and amber curves changing from moment to moment while the purple |ψ|² curve does not move.
04

T falls steeply with barrier width

For E < U the transmitted fraction through a barrier of full width 2a is exactly:

The law behind the T(E) plot. R = 1 − T.

Once 2ηa is larger than about 2, sinh(2ηa) ≈ e2ηa/2 and this reduces to:

The exponent carries the width.

At E = 0.30 eV and U = 0.50 eV, doubling the full width from 1.00 nm to 2.00 nm lowers T by a factor of 96, not 2. Raising U also lowers T: at 2a = 1.00 nm, U = 0.80 eV gives T = 0.27%, against 3.86% for 0.50 eV.

E U a

These sliders move the sim too.

See itRun the opening settings, then double the full width to 2.00 nm. Watch for: T dropping from 3.86% to 0.04%, a factor of about 100.
05

A step transmits nothing below U

Replace the barrier by a step, V = U for x ≥ 0, with the same E < U. Beyond the edge ψ is still a decaying exponential (κ in the sim's analytical panel), so |ψ|² reaches a short way into the step. There is no second edge to turn that tail back into a travelling wave. A real exponential carries no probability current, so no current leaves.

Penetration is not transmission: T counts current, not density.

Above the step one edge still reflects. At E = 0.60 eV and U = 0.50 eV, k₁ = 3.97 nm⁻¹ and k₂ = 1.62 nm⁻¹ give T = 82.3%.

See itSwitch to a step with E = 0.30 eV and U = 0.50 eV. Watch for: T = 0.00% and R = 100.00%, and |ψ|² dipping to zero at regular spacing on the left.
06

Above the barrier, T oscillates with energy

For E > U the wave inside is a travelling wave with wavenumber k₂, so the sinh becomes a sin:

The sin² has zeros, so T can reach 1.

Each edge reflects part of the wave, and T = 1 exactly when the two reflected parts cancel. That happens when sin(2k₂a) = 0: a whole number of half-wavelengths of the inner wave fits across the full width 2a. Between those energies T dips, but it is above 0.94 for 0.88 eV ≤ E ≤ 2.00 eV at the opening U and a.

See itSet E = 0.88 eV, with U = 0.50 eV and a = 0.50 nm. Watch for: T = 99.99% and a flat purple curve to the left of the barrier, because almost nothing is reflected.
07

The peaks move down and crowd as the barrier widens

Setting 2k₂a = nπ gives the energies of perfect transmission:

n = 1, 2, 3, …

En − U grows as n² and falls as 1/(2a)². Doubling a from 0.50 nm to 1.00 nm cuts every En − U by 4, so the peaks sit lower and closer together, and a third peak enters the energy range.

See itSet E = 0.59 eV, then double a from 0.50 nm to 1.00 nm. Watch for: T rising from 45.96% to 99.46%, because the first peak has moved down to 0.594 eV.
08

Where it matters

  • Scanning tunnelling microscope. A metal tip sits about half a nanometre above a surface, and the tunnel current through the gap changes by roughly a factor of ten for each 0.1 nm change in gap. That steepness lets it detect height changes far smaller than an atom.
  • Alpha decay. An alpha particle inside a heavy nucleus tunnels through a barrier it cannot climb. The exponential sensitivity to the barrier is why half-lives range from microseconds to billions of years.
  • Flash memory. In common NAND flash, electrons tunnel through a thin oxide layer to charge or discharge a storage gate.
Go deeper: the same exponential in a vacuum gap
  • With U − E = 4.5 eV, a typical metal work function, η = 10.9 nm⁻¹. Each extra 0.1 nm of gap lowers T by a factor of about 9.
  • A real tip–surface barrier is not rectangular, and a current needs a sum over many electrons. The plane-wave figures give the scale of the effect, not a prediction.
09

Summary

In one line. Below U the wave decays in the barrier and T falls steeply with width; above U, T oscillates and reaches 1 at En.

Key points

  • k = √(2mE)/ħ outside, η = √(2m(U − E))/ħ inside, and T + R = 1.
  • For E < U and 2ηa ≳ 2, T ≈ 16E(U − E)/U² · e−4ηa.
  • A step has T = 0 for E < U and T = 4k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂)² above.
  • A barrier with E > U has T = 1 at En = U + n²π²ħ²/(2m(2a)²).

Common mix-ups

  • "The electron borrows energy to cross the barrier." E is the same everywhere. The wave simply has a decaying part inside.
  • "Where |ψ|² is not zero, it is transmitted." In Step mode |ψ|² reaches past x = 0 while T = 0. T counts current that gets away.
  • "Above U, everything is transmitted." T reaches 1 only at En; a step still reflects 17.7% at E = 0.60 eV.

Things to try on your own

  • At E = 0.30 eV and U = 0.50 eV, find the a, in steps of 0.01 nm, where T first falls below 1%.
  • At a = 0.50 nm, find the E where T first reaches 99.9%, and compare it with E₁ = 0.876 eV.
